flavor: Hers. She read everything twice — contracts, can labels, your excuses. The apocalypse has fine print; she'd have read that too.
The 42, laminated by your own hand. Eleven years of on-time departures. Kept to remind the universe about punctuality — it never learned.
Butterscotch. Grandma doled them out like medals — good news, bad news, Tuesdays. This is the last one. It stays wrapped.
Dad's rule: dry socks are civilization. You laughed at him for twenty years. You carry the spare pair anyway.
Cracked screen, 2% forever. The last text is still on it. You've got it memorized, and you read it anyway.
Not yours. His. It still smells like dorm laundry and rain, and you are not ready for it to stop smelling like that.
Empty. The last real one got split three ways on the worst day, and it was somehow enough. The label gets read when you need the numbers to mean something.
Your handwriting, from when the routes still ran. Half schedules, half apocalypse patch notes. A magnum opus nobody asked for.
Hand-labeled in her block letters: 'FOR THE DRIVE.' No player. The songs are in your head anyway — her voice between the tracks.
Worn smooth. Grandpa flipped it for every big decision and ignored it every time. Heads or tails, it always lands on keep going.
A field guide to edible plants, ironically. Her copy — spine cracked at the mushroom chapter, margins full of corrections. She'd have loved being right about this.
His. Eight knives, every edge shaving-sharp — 'a dull knife is a tired cook.' He fed the whole block out of a kitchen the size of a closet.
Steel square, edges worn bright. Your father's. It built half the porches on Alder Street, and it has never measured wrong.
Brass compass, glass cracked but needle true. His father's. The glass broke on the last ridge they climbed together. The needle never lied, and neither did he.
One earcup cracked. Her voice came through it on the worst night the town ever had — 'stay with me, stay with me.' It still says it, when it's quiet.
Dented harmonica in C. Your brother's. He played every corner that would have him, and some that wouldn't. The corners are empty now.
A packet of seeds, her handwriting on the front. Plant after last frost. As if frost were still the problem.
